certainty_reasoning: Warren made the proposition; Sox reports West's refusal in terms of his discomfort with 'the possible implications', which is a refusal of the thing proposed and is recorded as such.
summary: On an 1889 trip to Wiesbaden and Rome, Warren told A. G. B. West that he wanted to share his life with 'an alter ego'. West, who had long intended to take Holy Orders, was not happy with the possible implications of such a relationship, and declined. Warren stayed devoted to him anyway - godfather to his sons, and in the end it was West's son who ran and inherited Warren's Maine house. The wooing of John Marshall followed.

sources.quote: During that trip Ned confided in West his desire to share his life with 'an alter ego'. … When stated that way, West was not happy with the possible implications of such a relationship.
sources.context: The 1889 Wiesbaden-Rome trip; between the sentences, Warren's worry about his companion 'seeming to be a rich man travelling with a friend when he was in reality accepting both salary and hospitality'.
sources.supports: The declined alter-ego proposition that preceded the Marshall wooing
